title: Tension-type headache
intro: Tension-type headache is the most common type of headache, causing a dull, pressing pain on both sides of the head, often described as a tight band. It is usually mild to moderate and does not stop daily activities. Simple painkillers, relaxation and good habits help, and frequent headaches can be treated preventively.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: The pain is typically steady rather than throbbing, felt on both sides of the head or around the forehead and neck, and does not worsen with routine activity. Nausea is absent or mild, and sensitivity to light or sound is slight, which helps distinguish it from migraine. Episodes last from thirty minutes to several days.

sections.heading: Causes and triggers
paragraphs: The exact cause is not known. Muscle tension in the neck and scalp, stress, poor sleep, skipped meals, dehydration, long periods of screen work with poor posture, eye strain and emotional strain are common triggers. Triggers differ between people, and a headache diary can help identify yours.

sections.heading: Treating an episode
paragraphs: Simple painkillers such as paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin, taken early in a dose recommended on the label, are usually effective. Rest, a warm or cool compress, gentle neck massage and relaxation can help. Avoid taking painkillers on more than about two or three days a week, since frequent use can cause medication-overuse headache.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: Regular sleep and meals, exercise, stress management, relaxation techniques, good posture and breaks from screens reduce frequency. Cognitive behavioural therapy and biofeedback help many people. For frequent or chronic headaches, a doctor may suggest a low-dose antidepressant taken daily, or other preventive treatment, and acupuncture has some supportive evidence.

sections.heading: When to seek urgent help
paragraphs: See a doctor promptly for a sudden, severe headache unlike any before, headache with fever and stiff neck, confusion, weakness, vision changes, difficulty speaking, after a head injury, or a new headache after age fifty. Also seek advice if headaches steadily worsen or disrupt daily life.

examples.title: Keeping a diary
examples.text: Imagine you have headaches several times a week. You could note times, stress, sleep, food and painkillers used, and review the pattern with your doctor.

examples.title: Adjusting your work setup
examples.text: Suppose headaches follow long hours at a screen. You might raise the monitor, take breaks every hour, stretch your neck and shoulders and have your eyes checked.
